title: HenTwin: A Multimodal Digital Twin Framework for Longitudinal Biological State Monitoring in Laying Hens
summary: Early-life monitoring in laying hens remains constrained by fragmented single-modality sensing and the absence of formal system-level state representations. HenTwin, a multimodal digital twin framework implemented as a five-layer IoT architecture, formalizes flock-level multimodal biological state dynamics from hatch through 25 weeks of age. A four-dimensional biological state vector integrating body surface temperature, acoustic energy entropy, band energy ratio, and optical-flow-based motion is defined, with the temperature-humidity index treated as an exogenous environmental input to preserve intervention capability. A discrete-time state transition model is estimated from 25 weeks of longitudinal multimodal data collected from 150 Lohmann LSL-Lite hens across five controlled rooms at the Atlantic Poultry Research Centre, Dalhousie University. The estimated transition matrix exhibits modality-specific persistence while remaining asymptotically stable. Perturbation analysis demonstrates that a sustained +2.0 THI increase produces a stable long-run acoustic entropy elevation of 0.54 nats, approximately one-quarter of the entire 1.87-nat developmental decline observed across the study period. Pettitt change-point detection identifies coordinated multimodal developmental state transitions at Weeks 12-14. Cross-room validation suggests that structural transition parameters are partially transferable across rooms, whereas environmental input sensitivity requires room-specific calibration, supporting a two-tier IoT deployment architecture. Leave-one-out cross-validation demonstrates consistent out-of-sample model performance. HenTwin takes a first step toward formal, state-aware digital twin inference in precision livestock farming.

AI.tldr: HenTwin is a five-layer IoT-based multimodal digital twin framework for laying hens that formalizes flock-level biological state dynamics using a four-dimensional state vector (temperature, acoustic entropy, band energy ratio, optical-flow motion) with THI as exogenous input, validated on 150 hens over 25 weeks.
AI.motivation: Early-life monitoring in laying hens is limited by fragmented single-modality sensing and lacks formal system-level state representations, motivating the need for a structured digital twin framework.
AI.method: A discrete-time state transition model is estimated from 25 weeks of longitudinal multimodal data from 150 Lohmann LSL-Lite hens. Perturbation analysis, Pettitt change-point detection, and cross-room validation with leave-one-out cross-validation are employed.
AI.result: The transition matrix is asymptotically stable with modality-specific persistence. A sustained +2.0 THI increase yields a 0.54-nat acoustic entropy elevation (~25% of the total 1.87-nat developmental decline). Coordinated multimodal transitions occur at Weeks 12-14, and structural parameters partially transfer across rooms while environmental sensitivity requires room-specific calibration.
AI.conclusion: HenTwin provides a first formal step toward state-aware digital twin inference in precision livestock farming, supporting a two-tier IoT deployment architecture.

title: Geographically Weighted Surrogate Models for Rapid Small-Area Chronic Disease Estimation
summary: Small-area estimation (SAE) enables researchers and policymakers to identify spatial disparities in health outcomes, but survey-based SAE products carry an inherent lag. Gold-standard estimates such as CDC PLACES are released roughly two years after the underlying survey data are collected, limiting their use for time-sensitive decision-making. This study evaluates the potential for machine learning (ML) to serve as a surrogate, learning the relationship between frequently updated area-level predictors and existing SAE outputs to generate timely, comparable estimates in years when SAE from surveys are unavailable or delayed. We evaluate several global and geographically weighted ML models for county-level SAE of ten chronic conditions across the US: COPD, asthma, heart disease, arthritis, cancer, depression, diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and stroke. Our findings suggest that geographically weighted ML frameworks like geographically weighted random forest and geographically weighted regression offer scalable and open data surrogates for rapidly generating SAE and supporting data driven decision making.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates machine learning models as surrogates for generating timely county-level small-area estimates (SAE) of ten chronic conditions in the US, finding that geographically weighted ML frameworks (geographically weighted random forest and geographically weighted regression) offer scalable alternatives to lagged survey-based estimates like CDC PLACES.
AI.motivation: Survey-based SAE products like CDC PLACES have an inherent ~2-year lag after data collection, limiting their use for time-sensitive decision-making. There is a need for timely, comparable estimates when survey-based SAE are unavailable or delayed.
AI.method: Evaluates multiple global and geographically weighted machine learning models for county-level SAE of ten chronic conditions (COPD, asthma, heart disease, arthritis, cancer, depression, diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, stroke), using frequently updated area-level predictors to learn the relationship to existing SAE outputs.
AI.result: Geographically weighted ML frameworks, specifically geographically weighted random forest and geographically weighted regression, demonstrate scalability and effectiveness as open data surrogates for rapidly generating SAE.
AI.conclusion: Geographically weighted ML approaches can serve as practical, timely surrogates for generating SAE and supporting data-driven decision-making in years when survey-based estimates are unavailable or delayed.

title: SymPerturb converts symptom-network structure into testable intervention priorities
summary: Symptom networks encode conditional dependence but do not by themselves identify causal or clinically actionable intervention targets. We introduce SymPerturb, a virtual-perturbation framework that distinguishes four primitive perturbation operators - virtual knockout, virtual knockdown, edge-level communication blocking and node-centred communication blocking - from three analytic procedures - virtual dosage perturbation, combination perturbation and sequence optimisation. The reference Gaussian implementation is embedded in a general location-scale map with symptom-specific target anchors, making explicit that zero anchoring and linked mean-variance attenuation are modelling choices. Seven utility outcomes quantify downstream efficacy, dose efficiency, breadth, cross-module reach, communication blocking, combination value and responsiveness; robustness is reported separately as an uncertainty diagnostic. Their direction-aligned, within-candidate-set weighted mean defines the virtual perturbation priority score (VPPS), which is a relative ranking rather than a transportable clinical utility score. In a known 22-node, four-module generating network, analytical efficacy agreed with 100,000-draw Monte Carlo estimates within 0.0024 standard deviations. The reported finite-sample VPPS results were generated with the original eight-component exploratory score and therefore require regeneration under the revised seven-utility-dimension definition. These simulations provide internal computational verification under model compatibility, not causal or external validation. SymPerturb is intended to generate auditable target hypotheses for longitudinal and experimental testing.

AI.tldr: SymPerturb is a virtual-perturbation framework for symptom networks that distinguishes four primitive perturbation operators and three analytic procedures to identify causal and clinically actionable intervention targets. It uses a Gaussian location-scale map with symptom-specific anchors, seven utility outcomes aggregated into a virtual perturbation priority score (VPPS) for relative ranking. The framework was computationally verified in a known 22-node, four-module network with strong agreement to Monte Carlo estimates, and is intended to generate auditable intervention hypotheses for future validation.
AI.motivation: Symptom networks encode conditional dependence between symptoms but do not by themselves identify causal or clinically actionable intervention targets, motivating the need for a framework that can infer which nodes or edges to perturb for therapeutic benefit.
AI.method: SymPerturb introduces four primitive perturbation operators (virtual knockout, virtual knockdown, edge-level and node-centred communication blocking) and three analytic procedures (virtual dosage perturbation, combination perturbation, sequence optimisation). It embeds in a general location-scale map with symptom-specific anchors, defines seven utility outcomes, and aggregates them via a direction-aligned weighted mean into the VPPS ranking score.
AI.result: In a known 22-node, four-module generating network, analytical efficacy agreed with 100,000-draw Monte Carlo estimates within 0.0024 standard deviations. Finite-sample VPPS results were generated under an older eight-component score and require regeneration under the revised seven-utility definition.
AI.conclusion: SymPerturb provides internal computational verification under model compatibility (not causal or external validation) and is intended to generate auditable target hypotheses for longitudinal and experimental testing.

title: But What Behavior?
summary: What is a natural behavior? I argue that the study of natural behaviors is often the study of the spontaneous behaviors of animals placed in quantifiably different environments. For behavioral generalists such as rodents, humans, and many other species, there may be no such definable construct as a native habitat or natural behavior, due to their successful abilities and needs to rapidly adapt to a wide range of different ecosystems. Instead of prioritizing naturalness, it may be more essential to determine objective outcome measures related to specific behaviors; i.e., which sequences of behaviors and adaptive mechanisms allow animals to survive and reproduce, across a range of dynamic or hazardous physical and social environments.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the concept of "natural behavior" by arguing that for behavioral generalists like rodents and humans, there is no definable native habitat or natural behavior. Instead, researchers should focus on objective outcome measures—identifying which behavioral sequences and adaptive mechanisms enable survival and reproduction across varied environments.
AI.motivation: The author questions the validity of studying "natural behaviors" in behavioral generalists, arguing that these species adapt too rapidly across diverse ecosystems for the concept of a native habitat or natural behavior to be meaningfully defined.
AI.method: A conceptual/argumentative analysis examining the definition of natural behavior, particularly for behavioral generalists, and proposing an alternative framework based on objective outcome measures rather than naturalness.
AI.result: The paper proposes that instead of prioritizing naturalness, researchers should determine objective outcome measures tied to specific behaviors, focusing on which behavioral sequences and adaptive mechanisms allow survival and reproduction across dynamic or hazardous environments.
AI.conclusion: The study of natural behavior may be better reframed as the study of spontaneous behaviors in quantifiably different environments, with a shift toward measurable behavioral outcomes rather than the ill-defined construct of naturalness.

title: EasyBCI Agent: Towards Universal Neural Data Preprocessing for Brain-Computer Interfaces
summary: Brain-computer interfaces translate neural activity into device commands, yet their performance hinges on preprocessing that remains manual, expert-dependent and poorly reproducible. Large language model agents can automate scientific coding, but existing systems lack the modality coverage, raw-data isolation, experience accumulation and domain oversight that neural preprocessing requires. We introduce EasyBCI, a two-phase LLM agent that plans and executes preprocessing pipelines for six signal types. A Plan Agent profiles each recording into a text-only Data Fingerprint that never exposes raw data to the model and selects a literature-grounded operator sequence. An Execution Agent generates, runs and self-corrects code until quality criteria are met, while a quality-gated experience system retains validated strategies as reusable skills. A domain expert intervenes at two decision gates, retaining human judgement where undetected error can invalidate downstream analyses. Evaluation on EEG with a fixed linear classifier shows that all five EasyBCI backbones preserve more task-relevant separability than the manual pipeline. Under same-backbone comparison, EasyBCI outperforms general-purpose coding agents on both label schemes for four of five configurations. EasyBCI extends to five additional modalities spanning nearly three orders of magnitude in sampling rate, producing complete reproducible pipelines with recorded decision provenance. These results indicate that domain-specific orchestration can bring auditable preprocessing within reach of laboratories lacking dedicated expertise, illustrating design principles applicable to AI agents in other scientific domains.

AI.tldr: EasyBCI is a two-phase LLM agent system (Plan Agent + Execution Agent) that automates neural signal preprocessing for six signal types, using a text-only Data Fingerprint to avoid raw-data exposure, a quality-gated experience system for reusable skills, and human expert gates for domain oversight. It outperforms manual pipelines and general-purpose coding agents on EEG classification tasks while extending to five additional modalities.
AI.motivation: BCI performance depends on preprocessing that remains manual, expert-dependent, and poorly reproducible. Existing LLM agents for scientific coding lack the modality coverage, raw-data isolation, experience accumulation, and domain oversight required for neural preprocessing.
AI.method: Two-phase LLM agent: (1) a Plan Agent profiles recordings into a text-only Data Fingerprint (no raw data exposure) and selects literature-grounded operator sequences; (2) an Execution Agent generates, runs, and self-corrects code until quality criteria are met. A quality-gated experience system retains validated strategies, and human experts intervene at two decision gates for domain oversight.
AI.result: On EEG with a fixed linear classifier, all five EasyBCI backbones preserve more task-relevant separability than the manual pipeline. It outperforms general-purpose coding agents on four of five configurations under same-backbone comparison. EasyBCI extends to five additional modalities spanning nearly three orders of magnitude in sampling rate, producing complete reproducible pipelines with recorded decision provenance.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific orchestration can bring auditable preprocessing within reach of labs lacking dedicated expertise, illustrating design principles (modality coverage, raw-data isolation, experience accumulation, domain oversight) applicable to AI agents in other scientific domains.

title: Improving scDiffusion with Sparsity-Biased Classifier-Free Guidance
summary: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has become an essential tool in modern cellular biology, and generating accurate synthetic scRNA-seq data is becoming increasingly important. Although diffusion models have achieved promising results in conditional scRNA-seq generation, existing guidance strategies, including classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance (CFG), rely on an unconditional branch trained to approximate the true marginal distribution, which may retain substantial gene-specific structure and limit guidance effectiveness. Inspired by recent work showing that diffusion models can be effectively guided using intentionally degraded references, we propose a sparsity-biased classifier-free guidance (SB-CFG) strategy for scRNA-seq generation. Rather than approximating the assumed "neutral" marginal distribution, SB-CFG introduces a deliberately under-informative sparse reference for the unconditional branch, removing gene identity while preserving only coarse sparsity statistics. This "bad" reference amplifies the contrast between conditional and unconditional predictions, leading to stronger and more effective guidance during sampling. We evaluated SB-CFG as a training-free sampling modification on five publicly available scRNA-seq datasets. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over standard CFG-based sampling in terms of marker gene expression fidelity, cell-type consistency, and sparsity preservation, indicating that SB-CFG better captures biologically meaningful gene expression patterns.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SB-CFG (sparsity-biased classifier-free guidance), a training-free sampling strategy for scRNA-seq generation that uses an intentionally under-informative sparse reference for the unconditional branch instead of approximating a neutral marginal distribution. This amplifies guidance contrast and improves generation quality across five scRNA-seq datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing guidance strategies (classifier guidance and CFG) for conditional scRNA-seq generation rely on an unconditional branch trained to approximate the true marginal distribution, which may retain substantial gene-specific structure and thereby limit the effectiveness of guidance. The authors seek a better guidance strategy inspired by work showing diffusion models can be effectively guided using intentionally degraded references.
AI.method: SB-CFG replaces the standard unconditional branch with a deliberately under-informative sparse reference that removes gene identity while preserving only coarse sparsity statistics. This "bad" reference amplifies the contrast between conditional and unconditional predictions during sampling, yielding stronger guidance. SB-CFG is applied as a training-free sampling modification.
AI.result: Evaluated on five public scRNA-seq datasets, SB-CFG consistently outperforms standard CFG-based sampling in marker gene expression fidelity, cell-type consistency, and sparsity preservation, indicating better capture of biologically meaningful gene expression patterns.
AI.conclusion: SB-CFG demonstrates that intentionally degraded references can serve as more effective guidance anchors than true marginal approximations for conditional scRNA-seq generation, improving biologically meaningful aspects of generated data without requiring retraining.

title: Critical Flicker Fusion Frequency As A Falsifiable Boundary Between Plastic And Non-Plastic Neural Systems
comment: 44 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables in Supplementary Material
summary: Experience-dependent neural plasticity is fundamental to adaptive behaviour, yet certain perceptual abilities resist modification despite extensive training. Critical flicker fusion frequency (CFFF), the threshold at which flickering light appears continuous, is a foundational constraint in visual temporal processing that shows exceptional within-individual stability in adults, contrasting sharply with the highly plastic spatial abilities processed through the same cortical pathways. This review proposes a hierarchical framework in which CFFF marks a boundary between plastic and non-plastic neural systems, operationalised via explicit falsification criteria. We examine whether CFFF stability reflects peripheral constraints, thalamocortical dynamics, cortical temporal filtering, or an integrated multi-level architecture, concluding it emerges from convergent constraints across processing levels. Within primary visual cortex, spatial properties show robust perceptual learning while temporal processing remains constrained, with temporal critical periods closing earlier than spatial ones. Critically, CFFF is unresponsive to non-specific cognitive training yet modifiable by perceptual-learning paradigms engaging the magnocellular-dorsal stream, a pattern defining rather than contradicting the plasticity boundary. Three principles reinforce this stability: a perceptual clock requires a stable reference frame for temporal binding; metabolic constraints render faster processing energetically prohibitive; and speed-accuracy trade-offs suggest selection optimised integration windows. We argue CFFF may serve as a trait marker whose links to working memory precision, metacognitive accuracy, and capacity limits remain testable hypotheses, not established findings. Understanding CFFF as a plasticity boundary illuminates how flexible cognitive systems operate within rigid sensory constraints.

AI.tldr: This review proposes that critical flicker fusion frequency (CFFF) represents a boundary between plastic and non-plastic neural systems, arguing that while spatial visual processing shows robust learning-based plasticity, temporal processing remains remarkably stable due to convergent constraints across peripheral, thalamocortical, and cortical levels, reinforced by functional principles of perceptual timing, metabolic efficiency, and optimized integration windows.
AI.motivation: To resolve the paradox that certain perceptual abilities resist modification despite extensive training—specifically, why CFFF (a foundational constraint in visual temporal processing) shows exceptional within-individual stability in adults, contrasting sharply with the highly plastic spatial abilities processed through the same cortical pathways.
AI.method: The paper presents a hierarchical framework with explicit falsification criteria, examining whether CFFF stability arises from peripheral constraints, thalamocortical dynamics, cortical temporal filtering, or an integrated multi-level architecture. It reviews evidence on perceptual learning, critical periods, training effects, and proposes three functional principles (stable reference frame for temporal binding, metabolic constraints, and speed-accuracy trade-offs) that reinforce the plasticity boundary.
AI.result: CFFF stability emerges from convergent constraints across multiple processing levels, not a single locus. Temporal critical periods close earlier than spatial ones. CFFF is unresponsive to non-specific cognitive training but modifiable by perceptual-learning paradigms engaging the magnocellular-dorsal stream. Three principles reinforce the stability of this perceptual clock.
AI.conclusion: CFFF may serve as a trait marker with testable (not established) links to working memory precision, metacognitive accuracy, and capacity limits. Understanding CFFF as a plasticity boundary illuminates how flexible cognitive systems operate within rigid sensory constraints.

title: metasignal: A Python Package for Comprehensive Metacognitive Analysis and Decision-Making
summary: Metasignal is an open-source Python package for signal detection theory (SDT) and metacognitive measurement. It implements the 17 metacognitive measures evaluated by Rahnev (2025), together with the reference variables d' (perceptual sensitivity), response criterion c (response bias), and mean confidence. The 17 measures comprise three meta-d' family estimates, meta-d', M-ratio, and M-difference; four nonparametric Type-2 measures, the Type-2 area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUC2), Gamma, Phi, and delta confidence, together with their eight SDT-normalized ratio and difference forms; and two model-based measures, meta-noise and meta-uncertainty. A single function computes the complete set from trial-level stimulus, response, and confidence arrays. `metasignal` currently supports binary (two-alternative) discrimination tasks, in which each trial's stimulus and response are coded with exactly two categories. The package also provides a command-line interface, group summaries, bootstrap confidence intervals, permutation tests, optional hierarchical Bayesian models, and information-theoretic measures. `metasignal` unifies these measures in a single platform to encourage broader metacognition research and adoption in decision-making studies.

AI.tldr: metasignal is an open-source Python package for signal detection theory and metacognitive measurement, implementing 17 metacognitive measures plus reference variables, with support for binary discrimination tasks, CLI, bootstrap, permutation tests, and hierarchical Bayesian models.
AI.motivation: To unify the many disparate metacognitive measures into a single accessible platform, encouraging broader research and adoption in decision-making studies.
AI.method: The package implements 17 metacognitive measures including meta-d' family estimates, nonparametric Type-2 measures (AUC2, Gamma, Phi, delta confidence) with SDT-normalized forms, and model-based measures (meta-noise, meta-uncertainty). A single function computes the full set from trial-level stimulus, response, and confidence arrays in binary discrimination tasks, with CLI, group summaries, bootstrap confidence intervals, permutation tests, and optional hierarchical Bayesian models.
AI.result: metasignal provides a complete, unified implementation of all 17 metacognitive measures evaluated by Rahnev (2025) along with reference variables d', c, and mean confidence, supporting extensive statistical analysis features.
AI.conclusion: metasignal offers a comprehensive and unified platform for metacognitive research, supporting binary discrimination tasks and providing tools for broader adoption in decision-making studies.

title: Quaternionic Response Geometry for Proteins: Toward a Noncommutative Theory of Ordered Deformations
comment: 43 pages, including 10 pages of appendices and 2 pages of references.5 figures. Submitted to Theory in Biosciences
summary: Protein function may depend on both endpoint conformations and the ordered deformation histories by which they are reached. This distinction is relevant to allostery, conformational switching, mutation-induced rearrangements, and epistatic effects, where different perturbation sequences may produce similar structures while retaining distinct internal transport histories. Current state- or endpoint-centered representations may not preserve this order-sensitive information. We therefore provide a foundation for descriptors of protein deformation trajectories that distinguish ordered histories even when endpoint conformations are similar. Such descriptors could support analyses of allosteric switching, mutation-order effects, conformational memory, and path-dependent response in molecular-dynamics trajectories, NMR ensembles, structural families, and outputs of geometric generative models. We propose a deformation-first geometric framework based on quaternionic frame transport along the protein backbone. Local backbone frames are lifted to quaternionic variables, with infinitesimal rotation encoded by \(Ω(\ell)=2\,q(\ell)^{-1}\partial_\ell q(\ell)\). Ordered concatenation of admissible deformation paths generates a noncommutative transport algebra, recording that deformation A followed by B need not be equivalent to B followed by A. From this ordered transport layer, we construct a spectral-response layer comprising a global Dirac-type operator, local spectral germs, a renormalized spectral density, and a mixed response form. A minimal realization on an idealized \(α\)-helix shows how localized pitch and bending perturbations can yield similar endpoint descriptors while preserving a nonzero order-memory signal. The framework separates an order-sensitive transport-memory sector, lost under a commutative shadow, from a spectral-response sector that remains visible.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a deformation-first geometric framework for protein trajectory analysis that captures order-sensitive information lost in endpoint- or state-based representations. Using quaternionic frame transport along the protein backbone, it constructs a noncommutative transport algebra where deformation order matters (A followed by B ≠ B followed by A), then builds a spectral-response layer with Dirac-type operators and spectral germs. A minimal α-helix realization demonstrates that order-memory signals persist even when endpoint descriptors appear similar.
AI.motivation: Protein function may depend on ordered deformation histories, not just endpoint conformations. Current state- or endpoint-centered representations cannot preserve order-sensitive information relevant to allostery, conformational switching, mutation-induced rearrangements, and epistatic effects where different perturbation sequences can produce similar final structures but retain distinct internal transport histories.
AI.method: The framework lifts local backbone frames to quaternionic variables, encoding infinitesimal rotation via Ω(ℓ)=2q(ℓ)⁻¹∂ℓq(ℓ). Ordered concatenation of deformation paths generates a noncommutative transport algebra capturing path-order. A spectral-response layer is built from a global Dirac-type operator, local spectral germs, a renormalized spectral density, and a mixed response form.
AI.result: A minimal realization on an idealized α-helix demonstrates that localized pitch and bending perturbations can yield similar endpoint descriptors while preserving a nonzero order-memory signal. The framework separates an order-sensitive transport-memory sector (lost under commutative shadow) from a spectral-response sector that remains visible.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a foundation for deformation trajectory descriptors that distinguish ordered histories even when endpoint conformations are similar, enabling analyses of allosteric switching, mutation-order effects, conformational memory, and path-dependent responses in various protein data sources including MD trajectories, NMR ensembles, structural families, and generative model outputs.

title: Resource depletion accelerates rate learning but not composition learning in patch foraging
summary: Foraging is a universal animal behavior that has increasingly attracted the interest of both experimentalists and theorists. Most prior models assume an animal knows the distribution of resources in its environment, but this structure must be learned as the animal explores its environment. Foraging can thus be regarded as a hierarchical inference problem. We develop a normative Bayesian account of an agent learning a patchy environment while exploiting it, and show that resource depletion shapes the levels of that hierarchy differently. Within a patch, depletion accelerates rate learning, since successive encounters occur at falling rates whose spacing pins down the initial rate. Across patches, composition learning, inferring the fraction of patches that are high yield, is slow, set by the number of patches sampled rather than the time spent in each, and unaffected by depletion once the rates are known. Reward-maximizing and information-seeking strategies therefore diverge, a forager resolving the composition underharvesting rich patches because learning it requires departures, most sharply early in exposure. When a fixed set of patches replenishes between visits, the reward-maximizing policy collapses onto a stable orbit over the high-yield patches, and the replenishment rate sets whether the forager maps the whole environment or locks onto a rich subset. Which departure rule maximizes intake is itself set by how variable the patches are, switching from counting prey to timing the gaps between them once richness varies by more than about a quarter. Learning the environment thus buys significant intake over learning a rule from reward alone, as long as its assumptions about depletion leave room for the truth.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a normative Bayesian framework for foraging where an agent must learn a patchy environment while exploiting it. The authors show that resource depletion accelerates within-patch rate learning but leaves cross-patch composition learning unaffected, causing reward-maximizing and information-seeking strategies to diverge. The optimal departure rule depends on patch variability, and learning the environment structure provides significant intake benefits over reward-based rule learning alone.
AI.motivation: Most prior foraging models assume animals know the resource distribution in their environment, but in reality this structure must be learned through exploration. Foraging should therefore be treated as a hierarchical inference problem where the agent simultaneously learns and exploits.
AI.method: The authors develop a normative Bayesian account of an agent learning a patchy environment (hierarchical inference) while exploiting it. They analyze how resource depletion differentially affects learning at different levels of the hierarchy—within-patch rate learning versus across-patch composition learning—and derive reward-maximizing vs. information-seeking policies.
AI.result: Within a patch, depletion accelerates rate learning because falling encounter rates pin down the initial rate. Across patches, composition learning is slow (set by number of patches sampled) and unaffected by depletion once rates are known. Reward-maximizing and information-seeking strategies diverge, with the diverge underharvesting rich patches early on. With replenishment, the optimal policy collapses to a stable orbit over high-yield patches. The departure rule switches from counting prey to timing gaps when patch richness varies by more than ~25%. Learning the environment yields significant intake benefits over reward-only rule learning.
AI.conclusion: Foraging is fundamentally a hierarchical inference problem where depletion shapes learning differently at different levels. The optimal foraging strategy depends critically on patch variability and replenishment rates, and explicitly learning environmental structure (rather than just learning a behavioral rule from reward) provides substantial benefits—provided the learning model's assumptions about depletion accommodate reality.

title: Quantifying the cost of network computations to unpack structure-function relationships in the brain
summary: The brain supports computations through coordinated patterns of activity on an underlying network. These networks---from microscale navigational circuits in insects to macroscale brain areas in humans---are organized in structured ways that are thought to support their function. We seek a unifying quantitative framework to understand how network structure shapes the computations a network can readily support. To do so, we frame computation as a goal-directed transition of activity and quantify its cost on a given network using control theory. We then define the distribution of costs across all possible transitions as a $\textit{computational affordance landscape}$ that encodes which computations a network structure readily supports. We apply this framework to a circuit model for how insects maintain a sense of direction and show that updating orientation is the least costly computation, with predicted inputs consistent with known circuitry. In the human brain, we find that the affordance landscape varies systematically with the functional role of each network. Sensory networks display more heterogeneous landscapes (reflecting their role in specialized information processing), whereas association networks display more homogeneous landscapes (reflecting their role in generalized information processing). In recurrent neural networks trained on cognitive tasks, we show that learning progressively increases landscape heterogeneity, reshaping the distribution of affordable computations. Generally, we establish a quantitative framework for studying relationships between structure and computation in neural circuits, with future applications extending to other biological and physical networks.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a "computational affordance landscape" framework that quantifies how network structure shapes the computations a network can readily support, using control theory to measure the cost of goal-directed activity transitions. Applied to insect navigation circuits, human brain networks, and trained recurrent neural networks, it reveals that structure biases which computations are affordable and that learning reshapes these landscapes.
AI.motivation: Neural networks across scales (from insect microcircuits to human macroscale brain areas) are organized in structured ways thought to support their function, but there is no unifying quantitative framework to understand how network structure shapes the computations a network can readily support.
AI.method: The authors frame computation as a goal-directed transition of activity and quantify its cost on a given network using control theory. They define the distribution of costs across all possible transitions as a "computational affordance landscape" that encodes which computations a network structure readily supports.
AI.result: In insect heading-direction circuits, updating orientation is the least costly computation, with predicted inputs matching known circuitry. In human brains, sensory networks display more heterogeneous affordance landscapes (specialized processing), while association networks display more homogeneous landscapes (generalized processing). In trained recurrent neural networks, learning progressively increases landscape heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a quantitative basis for studying structure-computation relationships in neural circuits, with potential applications extending to other biological and physical networks.

title: MPP-GNN: Subject-Adaptive Community Detection for fMRI-Based Alzheimer's Disease Classification
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging
summary: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is a widely used technique for studying the brain. Recent methods that utilize graph neural networks (GNNs) for analysis of brain functional connectivity have shown great potential for the classification of brain disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, these methods often assume a preset number of functional modules across all subjects, which overlooks inter-subject variability. In addition, the discovered modules are rarely used to directly guide the learned connectivity patterns. Here, to address these issues, we propose a Meta Probabilistic Pooling GNN (MPP-GNN). We frame the model's task as a coupled, bilevel optimization that performs adaptive graph partitioning hierarchically to discover subject-specific modules and then uses the discovered brain modules as an explicit prior to guide edge refinement and representation learning. We validate MPP-GNN on two public datasets for AD classification, achieving the highest AUC in comparison to established baselines for both datasets. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that MPP-GNN shows significant alignment with the canonical functional-network organization defined by the Yeo brain atlas and reveals a network-level dedifferentiation pattern for AD.

AI.tldr: MPP-GNN is a graph neural network framework that uses meta probabilistic pooling to discover subject-specific brain functional modules and uses them as priors to guide edge refinement, achieving state-of-the-art Alzheimer's disease classification and aligning with canonical brain network organization.
AI.motivation: Existing GNN-based fMRI methods assume a preset number of functional modules across all subjects, ignoring inter-subject variability, and discovered modules are rarely used to directly guide learned connectivity patterns.
AI.method: Frames the task as a coupled bilevel optimization that performs hierarchical adaptive graph partitioning to discover subject-specific brain modules, then uses these modules as explicit priors to guide edge refinement and representation learning in a GNN.
AI.result: Achieves the highest AUC on two public AD classification datasets compared to established baselines, demonstrates significant alignment with the Yeo brain atlas, and reveals a network-level dedifferentiation pattern for Alzheimer's disease.
AI.conclusion: Subject-specific module discovery with explicit module-guided representation learning improves both classification performance and neurobiological interpretability in fMRI-based brain disorder analysis.

title: Bits per Spike as a Betting Game: An Interpretable Unit for Held-Out Log-Likelihood in Neural Data Analysis
summary: Held-out log-likelihood is the standard currency for comparing statistical models of neural spike trains, and is often reported as bits per spike relative to a homogeneous Poisson baseline. The units of this metric are difficult to reason about: it is rarely obvious whether an improvement of, say, $0.34$ bits per spike is a large effect or a negligible one. This note develops an interpretation of held-out log-likelihood borrowed from game-theoretic statistics. A fitted model $Q$ is treated as a player who bets on each upcoming observation at prices set by a baseline model $B$. Under the optimal (Kelly) betting strategy the player's contract function is exactly the likelihood ratio $q/b$, and the expected log-likelihood ratio $L$ is the exponential growth rate of the player's wealth. Because the wealth process is a nonnegative martingale under the null hypothesis that $B$ generated the data, Ville's inequality turns it into an anytime-valid test: the baseline may be rejected at level $α$ as soon as wealth exceeds $1/α$. This yields a simple summary statistic, the time to significance $τΔ= -Δ\log(α) / L$, which is the amount of held-out recording needed on average to reject the baseline at level $α$. Since $τ$ is a strictly decreasing function of $L$, it ranks models identically to bits per spike; it is not a new statistic but a more interpretable unit for an existing one, expressed in seconds of recording rather than in bits. We illustrate the construction on head-direction cells recorded in mouse anterior thalamus, where a generalized linear model reaches significance against a homogeneous Poisson baseline in roughly $120$ ms of held-out data for a strongly tuned cell and roughly $11$ s for a moderately tuned cell.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a more interpretable unit for held-out log-likelihood in neural spike train models. By framing model comparison through game-theoretic betting (where a fitted model bets against a baseline at likelihood-ratio prices), the authors connect expected log-likelihood ratio to exponential wealth growth, enabling anytime-valid hypothesis testing via Ville's inequality. They propose "time to significance" — the recording duration needed to reject the baseline at a given significance level — which ranks models identically to bits per spike but is expressed in seconds of recording. Demonstrated on head-direction cells where significant improvement over Poisson baseline occurs in ~120 ms (strongly tuned) to ~11 s (moderately tuned).
AI.motivation: Bits per spike, the standard metric for comparing neural spike train models, is difficult to interpret — it is unclear whether a given improvement (e.g., 0.34 bits/spike) is large or negligible. The paper seeks a more interpretable unit for the same statistic without introducing a new metric.
AI.method: The fitted model Q is cast as a bettor using the Kelly criterion, wagering at prices set by a baseline model B. The contract function is the likelihood ratio q/b, and the log-likelihood ratio L is the exponential growth rate of the gambler's wealth. Since wealth is a nonnegative martingale under the null (data from B), Ville's inequality provides an anytime-valid test: reject baseline at level α when wealth exceeds 1/α. This gives a time-to-significance metric τ = -Δ log(α)/L, converting log-likelihood into expected seconds of held-out recording.
AI.result: Applied to head-direction cells in mouse anterior thalamus, a GLM achieves significance against a homogeneous Poisson baseline in ~120 ms of held-out data for a strongly tuned cell and ~11 s for a moderately tuned cell. The metric ranks models identically to bits per spike but offers a more tangible, experiment-time-based interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Time to significance is not a new statistic but a more interpretable unit for held-out log-likelihood, grounded in game-theoretic statistics. It frames model comparison in terms of recording time needed to establish significance, making the practical impact of model improvements directly understandable.

title: Fleming-Viot Selection of the Yaglom Limit for Age-Structured Bellman-Harris Processes, with Application to Livestock Epidemic Surveillance
summary: In this paper, we construct a Fleming-Viot particle system for a class of subcritical Bellman-Harris processes. We prove that it selects the Yaglom limit at a polynomial rate in the number of particles. Since lifetimes are non-exponential, the population size is not Markov, and the analysis must therefore be carried out on the space of age configurations. In this setting, the Lyapunov functions used for Galton-Watson processes are no longer norm-like. Nevertheless, we establish a Yaglom theorem that strengthens the classical result: the conditional laws converge in total variation at an exponential rate, with decay rate given by the Malthusian parameter. We also prove that the drift condition, which links the hazard rate to the offspring law, is necessary within a natural class of Lyapunov functions, showing that it is a feature of the measure-valued lift rather than a defect of the estimates. Finally, we illustrate the estimator through an application to livestock epidemic surveillance, where the Yaglom limit is the null distribution of a change-detection test.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs a Fleming-Viot particle system for subcritical Bellman-Harris processes, proving it selects the Yaglom limit at a polynomial rate. The analysis is carried out on age configurations (not population size) since lifetimes are non-exponential. The authors establish a strengthened Yaglom theorem with exponential convergence in total variation at the Malthusian rate, show the drift condition is necessary, and demonstrate an application to livestock epidemic surveillance.
AI.motivation: To extend the Fleming-Viot particle system approach for selecting Yaglom limits from Galton-Watson processes to the more general Bellman-Harris processes where lifetimes are non-exponential, making the population size non-Markovian and requiring analysis on age configuration spaces. This provides particle-system-based estimators for conditional rare-event probabilities in a broader class of branching processes.
AI.method: The authors construct a Fleming-Viot particle system on the space of age configurations for subcritical Bellman-Harris processes. They employ Lyapunov function techniques adapted to the age-configuration setting (since standard norm-like Lyapunov functions from the Galton-Watson case no longer apply), establish the Yaglom theorem with exponential total variation convergence at a rate given by the Malthusian parameter, and prove necessity of the drift condition within a natural class of Lyapunov functions.
AI.result: The Fleming-Viot particle system selects the Yaglom limit at polynomial rate in the number of particles. A strengthened Yaglom theorem is proven with exponential convergence in total variation, with decay rate given by the Malthusian parameter. The drift condition is shown to be necessary within a natural class of Lyapunov functions. An application to livestock epidemic surveillance demonstrates the estimator's practical utility for change-detection testing.
AI.conclusion: The particle-system framework for Yaglom limit selection extends successfully to Bellman-Harris processes, with the measure-valued lift approach requiring the drift condition as an intrinsic feature. The method provides a practically useful estimator with demonstrated application to epidemic surveillance.

title: Multi-Source Multi-View Graph Domain Adaptation with Hyperbolic Residual Encoding for Cross-Site MDD Identification from rs-fMRI
summary: Cross-site identification of major depressive disorder (MDD) from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) is hindered by inter-site distribution shifts and heterogeneous functional connectivity (FC) views. These views capture complementary neural relationships but exhibit distinct site biases and graph topologies, complicating alignment without sacrificing disease-relevant information or cross-view consistency. Existing studies largely treat multi-view connectome learning and cross-site adaptation separately. To the best of our knowledge, few studies have jointly modeled multiple FC views under multi-source unsupervised domain adaptation for cross-site rs-fMRI-based MDD classification. We construct Pearson correlation, sparse representation, and Granger causality graphs, each encoded by a view-specific graph attention network. Dual-stream adaptive fusion explicitly integrates pairwise cross-view interactions, followed by lightweight hyperbolic residual encoding for curvature-aware representation refinement. Class-wise Cauchy--Schwarz alignment reduces inter-source and source-target discrepancies, complemented by adversarial learning, information maximization, and confidence-aware pseudo-labeling. Across seven unlabeled target domains, our framework achieves 73.60% mean accuracy and 71.90% AUC, demonstrating effective generalization under heterogeneous acquisition conditions. These results highlight the effectiveness of unified heterogeneous-view modeling, curvature-aware refinement, and multi-source domain adaptation for cross-site MDD identification.The source code is at https://github.com/OPUS-Lightphenexx/MM-HyperGDA

It achieves 73.60% mean accuracy and 71.90% AUC across seven unlabeled target domains.
